content: Sideburns, also referred to colloquially as side-whiskers or sideboards in the United Kingdom, are defined as patches of facial hair that grow on the sides of a man’s face, specifically in front of the ears. The term sideburns originated as a 19th-century alteration of the word burnsides, named after Ambrose Burnside, a historical figure known for his distinctive facial hairstyle. Burnside’s style featured thick sideburns connected by a mustache, while the chin remained clean-shaven. Sideburns are not confined to a specific length or shape, and their variations throughout history are numerous. They can be thin or wide, voluminous or neatly trimmed, cropped flat, flared outward, or tapered to a point. They may terminate at mid-ear level or extend further down the jawline. The term sideburns is broad and encompasses other distinct facial hair styles, such as mutton chops and friendly mutton chops. Mutton chops are sideburns that extend down to the corners of the mouth, resembling the shape of a cut of mutton. Friendly mutton chops, on the other hand, connect both sideburns with a mustache, creating a style reminiscent of Ambrose Burnside’s own facial hair. Sideburns can be paired with other facial hair styles, such as a mustache or goatee. However, when the hair extends from ear to ear via the chin, it ceases to be classified as sideburns and instead becomes a beard or a chin curtain. Historically, sideburns gained popularity in the early 19th century following the clean-shaven trends of the 18th century. This resurgence in facial hair fashion eventually spread to other parts of the world, including Japan. During the 19th century, sideburns were often more extravagant than those seen today, resembling what we now recognize as modern-day mutton chops. However, like beards, sideburns fell out of favor in the early 20th century but experienced a revival in the 1960s and 1970s, particularly among younger generations. Pointed sideburns, in particular, became emblematic of the gay club scenes in cities such as San Francisco and Sydney, Australia. Due to their diverse historical associations, sideburns can be perceived as either a symbol of Victorian-era conservatism or 1970s-style rebellion. In contemporary times, sideburns enjoy moderate popularity, with dedicated groups of enthusiasts forming and thriving, especially with the advent of the internet. In some cultures, sideburns hold unique significance. For example, indigenous men in Mexico who shave their heads but grow long sideburns, as well as Colombians who wear long sideburns without other facial hair, are said to sport a style known as balcarrotas. Notable historical figures known for their distinctive sideburns include Henrik Ibsen (1828–1906), Franz Joseph I of Austria (1830–1916), Miguel Grau Seminario (1834–1879), and W. S. Gilbert (1836–1911).
